topics.topic: The clock, capture timing, representation, and precision used for retention cutoff comparisons
questions: Which clock supplies this instant, in what representation is it compared with the backup's recorded UTC instant, and is the single cutoff reading taken before any file is inspected?
From which clock is the third step's cutoff instant read: the UTC wall clock, the process monotonic clock, or a time captured earlier in the run?
What exact representation and precision does Registry use for recorded UTC instants and comparisons at retention boundaries?

quotes:
Every duration in this decision — the 8 hours, the 30, 15 and 10
   minutes, the 60 seconds — is measured by the process's monotonic clock,
   which a change of the wall clock does not move and which counts the time
   the host or its VM was suspended, so a session does not outlive a
   suspension; instants Registry records
   and the 03:00 of A18 are UTC wall-clock time.

Third, whatever the second step did, it deletes every kept
   backup made more than 30 × 24 hours before the instant this step starts,
   one cutoff for the whole step — a backup made exactly 30 × 24 hours before
   it is kept.
judgement.divergence: One implementation reads one precise UTC wall-clock instant when step three starts; another reuses an earlier run instant, uses monotonic elapsed time, or rounds UTC instants differently. The owner sees different backups retained at the boundary.
judgement.why: The text fixes the retention threshold and one-cutoff rule but does not identify the cutoff's clock reading or precision, so the changed retention passage leaves observable boundary behavior open.

witness.initial: A kept backup has a recorded UTC instant near the 720-hour boundary, and the host wall clock is changed before rotation starts.
events: Registry starts the third backup step.
Registry compares the kept backup's recorded instant with the retention cutoff.
outcomes: A UTC wall-clock cutoff with subsecond precision deletes the backup as more than 720 hours old.
A monotonic, earlier-captured, or rounded cutoff keeps the backup at the boundary.
witness.observer: The owner listing the backup location
basis:
It
   records, readable without its key, its instant, the release that made it,
   the last audit sequence number its store ever wrote — kept apart from the
   entries (A15; M12 AuditSequence), 0 for a store that never wrote one, whatever the log now
   holds — and a digest of the key it was
   made with (never the key); its age is counted from that instant.

Third, whatever the second step did, it deletes every kept
   backup made more than 30 × 24 hours before the instant this step starts,
   one cutoff for the whole step — a backup made exactly 30 × 24 hours before
   it is kept.

topics.topic: When an oversized upload without a trustworthy over-limit declared length is refused
questions: Must “a file over the limit is refused before it is read” be narrowed to requests whose trustworthy declared length is already over the limit, with undeclared or underdeclared uploads read through byte 52,428,801 before refusal?
For an oversized upload whose declared length is absent or not over the limit, is it refused before any file byte is read or only after Registry reads the limit plus one byte?
For an upload with no trustworthy over-limit declared length, is it refused before Registry reads any file byte or only after Registry has read the limit plus one byte?

quotes:
nothing in it is executed or evaluated, and
   a file over the limit is refused before it is read.

The limit is counted
   over the bytes Registry receives, never over a length the request
   declares: a declared length over the limit is refused before any byte is
   read; otherwise Registry reads the upload up to one byte more than the
   limit and refuses it as soon as it holds more than the limit, whatever
   length was declared or whether one was.
judgement.divergence: An oversized upload without an over-limit declared length is either refused before any byte is read or refused only after byte 52,428,801 is read; the uploading client and host operator observe the difference.
judgement.why: The first passage requires every oversized file to be refused before reading, while the second requires reading through the limit plus one unless the declared length itself is over the limit.

Must the import also apply A02's object-kind and numeric-characteristic checks to values brought in from the file, or does it apply A02 only to names and aliases supplied in the mapping?

quotes: For an accepted file, the file's digest, the SHA-256 of its bytes, which Registry computes and never takes from a caller.

The closure first and alone: when it exists, `import_closed` is the answer (rule 8; Conventions, "Stages"). Then the upload the confirmation bound — that session's upload of that number, not merely bytes of that digest: when it is no longer kept, `file_not_kept` is answered alone, there being no bytes to check again (rule 2). Otherwise every other stage (6) failure is answered together, the kept bytes' digest computed again: the picks checked again — any conflict, malformed record or missing value, or no pick at all — refuse the whole import (rule 6); the values the confirmation bound and nothing else; the projects link to the Customers it makes (R0-80).
precedent.why: State 5 selects SHA-256 over the uploaded bytes and binds confirmation to the session upload number as well as the digest, so replacing the bytes is refused even if their digest collides.
